passage: Nirmala, you said you can't do spreadsheet formulas. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, at the post office in Amritsar, the year the computers came. Everyone younger learned fast. I sat there resenting the machine, saying, "I can't do this. I'm not a computer person." One evening the postmaster, an old Sikh gentleman, heard me and said, "Gurpreet, you can't do it yet. What will you try next?" That word annoyed me, honestly. But I went home and wrote on a paper: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day." It wasn't magic. My first method, copying from the manual, didn't help at all. Harjit's way did. So, Nirmala: yet, and then, what will you try?

qa.q: What did young Gurpreet write on the paper at home?
qa.a: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day."

qa.q: Why did the word "yet" annoy young Gurpreet at first?
qa.a: Gurpreet was full of resentment toward the machine and felt stuck; "yet" sounded too easy, as if it brushed aside how hard it felt.

qa.q: Which choice made "yet" actually work for Gurpreet?
qa.a: Pairing it with a concrete next step, and switching from the manual to Harjit's way when the first method failed.

qa.q: What might Nirmala take from this story?
qa.a: Nirmala may see that struggling with formulas now doesn't close the future, and that the useful question is what to try next.

grounding: An elder recalls turning 'I can't' into 'I can't yet' at twenty-five and pairing it with a better strategy.

passage: Maria had failed her driving test in Panaji twice, both times on the slope start, and her new job at a clinic in Mapusa needed her driving in three weeks. The monsoon had turned the practice ground to mud. After the second fail she sat in Simran's car in the rain and said, "I can't do this. I'm just not a driver." Simran didn't argue. "You can't do slope starts yet. What haven't you tried?" Maria wiped her eyes, annoyed. Then she thought. She had only ever practised on flat roads. She'd never used the handbrake method the instructor mentioned. The next morning, rain still falling, she found a quiet sloping lane near the church and did twenty slope starts with the handbrake. Nineteen didn't roll back.

qa.q: How many of Maria's slope starts didn't roll back?
qa.a: Nineteen of twenty.

qa.q: Why was Maria annoyed when Simran said "yet"?
qa.a: After two fails and with a deadline looming, she felt defeated, and "yet" seemed to brush past how bad she felt.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Simran's question about what she hadn't tried; Maria chose to practise on a real slope with the handbrake method instead of flat roads.

qa.q: How might Simran feel seeing Maria practise in the rain?
qa.a: Simran may feel glad that a short question helped, and quietly proud of a friend who turned tears into a plan.

grounding: An adult under time pressure reframes 'I can't drive' as 'not yet' and finds a better practice strategy.

passage: At the Nariman Point office, Hrithik's first client presentation had gone badly: he lost his place, read from the slides, and watched the client check his phone. Hrithik almost rolled his eyes; it sounded like a poster. But that night he wrote two lines: "Can't present yet. Try: practise out loud three times, use cue cards not slides." He rehearsed in the empty conference room, twice to the wall and once to Pankaj. The next presentation wasn't perfect. But he didn't read from the slides, and the client asked two questions.

passage:
Dear Seema,
After three months of our "growth mindset" campaign, I want to share honestly what I'm seeing on my team. The posters are up. People repeat "mistakes are how we learn" in meetings. But when Arjun made an error in the vendor report last week, he was named in the all-staff email, and since then nobody on my floor has asked a question in a meeting. My analysts are booked on back-to-back client work; there is no hour in the week to learn the new tools we keep praising. And the only feedback they get is the annual review. I don't think the slogan is wrong. I think we're asking people to take risks without time, feedback or protection. Could we pilot two hours of protected learning a week and monthly one-to-ones on my team?
Regards,
Leela

qa.q: What happened after Arjun's error in the vendor report?
qa.a: He was named in the all-staff email, and since then nobody on the floor has asked a question in a meeting.

qa.q: Why might Leela's analysts stay silent despite the posters?
qa.a: They likely fear being publicly named like Arjun, so the risk of speaking feels bigger than any slogan's promise.

qa.q: What choice does Leela propose, and why might it work better than more posters?
qa.a: Two protected learning hours a week and monthly one-to-ones, which give the time and feedback that make learning actually possible.

qa.q: How might Arjun have experienced the all-staff email?
qa.a: Arjun probably felt embarrassed and exposed, learning that mistakes are punished whatever the posters say.

grounding: A manager notices growth slogans failing because the team lacks time, feedback and safety to learn.

passage: Chaitanya, you asked what I'd do differently as a new manager. Here's one. When I took over the support team, I was obsessed with growth mindset. I put "Not yet!" stickers on every monitor. I said "fail forward" in every stand-up. And nothing changed. People still hid mistakes. Then one of my juniors said something I won't forget: "Pradeep, you say mistakes are fine, but the dashboard turns red for every late ticket, and we get no time to practise the new system." She was right. I was selling the idea without building the conditions. So we dropped ticket targets for one afternoon a week, made that afternoon for practice, and I started ten-minute feedback chats. The stickers are still there. Now they mean something.

qa.q: What did Pradeep put on every monitor?
qa.a: "Not yet!" stickers.

qa.q: Why did the team keep hiding mistakes despite the stickers?
qa.a: The red dashboard still punished every late ticket and there was no time to practise, so admitting mistakes felt unsafe whatever the stickers said.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Pradeep change?
qa.a: A junior pointing out the gap; Pradeep freed one afternoon a week for practice and began short feedback chats.

qa.q: How might the junior feel seeing the changes after speaking up?
qa.a: She would likely feel heard and more trusting, since speaking honestly led to real change rather than trouble.

grounding: A manager realises growth slogans do nothing without time and feedback, and builds the conditions.

passage: I'm Ira, and I manage the design team at a small publishing house. Our director gave a talk in January about "embracing challenge" and "loving feedback". I watched Pema, one of my best illustrators, nod through it. Over the next weeks I kept an eye on her. She didn't try the new digital painting style the director had praised. When I asked why, she said lightly, "No time. The deadlines are the same." I noticed she hadn't had feedback on her work since her probation ended. I can't know everything she was feeling. But I stopped repeating the slogans. I blocked Friday afternoons for practice and sat with her every other week to look at her sketches. By March she'd done a whole cover in the new style, and asked me what to fix.

qa.q: What did Ira block Friday afternoons for?
qa.a: Practice.

qa.q: What might Pema's light answer, "No time", suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She may have felt the new style was a risk she couldn't afford with the same deadlines and no feedback, so trying it seemed unsafe.

qa.q: Which choices by Ira made the new style possible?
qa.a: Blocking practice time and giving regular feedback on sketches, instead of repeating the director's slogans.

qa.q: How might the director see the change if shown Pema's new cover?
qa.a: The director might realise that talks alone didn't do it, and that time and feedback turned the idea into real work.

grounding: A manager sees that growth talk fails without time and feedback, and builds both for a team member.

Mentor's note, Dr Ankita, first-year mentoring, 18 September
Jyoti came to my office today, her third visit in two weeks, each time asking whether the admissions office double-checks ranks after joining. Today she finally said what she meant: she believes she got in through a mistake or pure luck, and that it will show soon. Her quiz scores are in the top third of the batch. When I pointed this out, she said, "Those quizzes are easy; the others aren't even trying." She compares herself only with the two strongest students in her section. She looked tired and kept twisting her ID lanyard.
What I did: I asked her to write down three pieces of evidence of her own ability before our next meeting, and invited her to the Thursday peer circle where seniors talk about their first year.

qa.q: Where are Jyoti's quiz scores in the batch?
qa.a: In the top third of the batch.

qa.q: Why does Jyoti dismiss her good quiz scores?

passage: Kavitha, sit. You think you're the only one who feels lost at that college? When I went to Madras for my M.A., I was the first in my family to finish school, let alone university. My father drove a bus in Salem. Everyone in my class knew words I'd never heard: office hours, viva, citation. They called professors by name and argued with them. I thought, these people belong here, and I've sneaked in. I had first-class marks, but I sat at the back and never spoke. Then a girl from Tirunelveli, also the first in her family, found me in the library and said, "Shalini, you also don't know what a viva is, no?" We laughed so hard. We learned the codes together. That friendship made me stay, Kavitha. Find your people.

passage: Parul's scholarship covered fees, not extras, so when her Delhi classmates booked the orientation trip to the hills, she said she had "family things" and stayed in the hostel. Her parents, who had never been to college, asked on the phone whether she'd made friends. "Yes," she lied. On the empty weekend she found a notice: "First-generation students' circle, Room 12, Sunday." She almost didn't go. Harish, a third-year from a farming family in Bihar, was running it. "LMS is just the website for assignments," he said. "Nobody tells us. So we tell each other." She stayed two hours.

passage: In her first month at the college on College Street, Bidisha noticed everything that marked her out. Her classmates spoke up easily in seminars and chatted about summer internships their parents had arranged. Her father ran a small cycle-repair shop in Howrah; nobody at home knew what a seminar was. Her first-term marks were among the best in the class, but she still ate lunch alone and felt like a guest who had come to the wrong house. One evening her roommate Lakshmi, from a fishing family near Chennai, admitted to feeling the same. "I thought it was just me," Lakshmi said. qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt relief, since what seemed a lonely weakness turned out to be common among students like them.

grounding: A first-generation student feels out of place despite top marks, and finds community with others like her.

passage: In her first month at the consultancy in Madrid, Layla was always the last to leave. She rehearsed every meeting, rechecked every chart three times, and wrote answers to questions nobody would ask. When her first client presentation went well, Diego, who'd joined with her, said, "You were brilliant." Layla shook her head. "Only because I prepared for eleven hours. If I hadn't, they'd have seen I don't know anything." She felt a wave of relief at having got away with it, and a knot of fear about the next one. Diego frowned. "You've done that for every meeting. Has one ever gone badly?" Layla thought. None had. "That's because I overprepared," she said. Diego sighed. "Or because you're good."

qa.a: Eleven hours.

"Yamini, you're one of the sharpest people on this team," he said. "Would you believe that if you'd left at six?" She didn't answer. She didn't know.

passage: The team restructuring was due on Friday, and the manager had asked Parveen to lead the new quality unit. qa.a: Tanvir may feel touched and glad that sharing an old vulnerability helped, and perhaps more willing to share it with others.

grounding: An adult tells a mentor about feeling like a fraud and learns that capable people feel the same, which reduces shame.

passage: Okay, Amandeep, the honest answer to how I survived my first year at the firm? I told someone. For months I'd been sure I was the weakest architect there, that my designs only got approved because the partners were being kind to the new girl. I told nobody. I'd go home and replay every comment. Then one night at a friend's birthday, my old classmate Meher asked how work was, and I just said it: "I think I'm a fraud." Meher burst out laughing, not at me, and said, "Chandrika, I've felt that every day at the hospital for two years." Then two other people at the table said the same. I cried in the car afterwards, but a good cry. The voice still comes sometimes. But it's quieter when you know half the room hears it too.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say when Meher asked about work?
qa.a: "I think I'm a fraud."

qa.q: Why was it a good cry in the car afterwards?
qa.a: After months of hiding the fear, hearing friends admit the same brought relief; the shame loosened once the secret was shared.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chandrika's first year?
qa.a: Answering Meher's question honestly at the birthday instead of saying work was fine, which let others share the same feeling.

qa.q: How might Meher have felt when Chandrika said it?
qa.a: Meher probably felt instant recognition, even relief, and laughed because the confession matched exactly what Meher had been carrying.

grounding: An adult admits feeling like a fraud to friends and finds many capable people feel the same, which quiets the shame.

passage:
Friday
Got 17 out of 20 in the Hindi test. I hid it in the back of my geography book. Papa only smiles when it's 20. When I got 20 in maths, he took me for ice cream and hugged me and told Dadi on the phone. When I got 16 last month he didn't say anything at dinner, just looked at the paper and put it down. Nikita didi says he's just busy. But I think he likes me more when I get full marks. Tomorrow he'll ask about the Hindi test. I'll say it's not back yet. My stomach feels funny writing this. I wish he'd hug me even when it's 17.
Gautam

qa.q: Where did Gautam hide the Hindi test?
qa.a: In the back of the geography book.

qa.q: Why does Gautam's stomach feel funny writing this?
qa.a: Gautam worries that Papa's love depends on full marks, and feels guilty about planning to hide the test.

qa.q: What could help Gautam and Papa most?
qa.a: Gautam telling Nikita didi or Papa how it feels, and Papa showing warmth for effort and for Gautam, not only for 20 out of 20.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he read this diary?
qa.a: Papa would probably be shocked and sad to learn that his silence felt like love being taken away, when he may only have been busy.

grounding: A child who sees his father warm only after full marks hides a lower score and feels loved for performance.

passage: In Kurnool, results day at the government school meant a line of mothers outside the gate. Nandini came out with her progress card held tight against her chest. Second rank. Her mother, Farida, reached for it, read it, and her face went still. "Second? Who came first?" "Sneha," Nandini said quietly. Farida handed the card back without a word and walked ahead to the bus stop. At home she didn't make the kheer she'd made last term, when Nandini came first. That night Nandini tore out the page of her maths notebook with a red cross on it and hid it under the mattress. She lay awake, wondering if Ammi would have hugged her if she'd been first.

qa.q: What rank did Nandini get?
qa.a: Second rank.

qa.q: Why did Nandini hide the maths page with the red cross?
qa.a: She has learned that less than first brings silence instead of warmth, so she hides any mistake that might cost her Ammi's affection.

qa.q: What could Farida do differently next results day?
qa.a: Hug Nandini and ask how she feels before looking at the rank, so her love is clearly not tied to coming first.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Farida walks ahead to the bus stop?
qa.a: It feels like being left behind; the silence and the missing kheer tell Nandini her mother's warmth depends on the rank.

grounding: A child whose mother responds only to top rank feels loved for performance and begins hiding mistakes.

passage: In their flat in Kraków, Olga's mother, Ines, kept a board on the fridge with every test score Olga brought home. Only the top marks went up; anything less was folded away in a drawer, with a sigh. On evenings when a top mark went on the board, Ines baked honey cake and called Olga her little star. On other evenings, dinner was quiet. One Thursday Olga got a low mark in spelling. She didn't bring it home. She threw it in the bin at the tram stop, then felt so sick she couldn't eat her lunch. When Ines asked about spelling, Olga said, "We didn't have it." Later, in bed, she hugged her pillow and whispered, "Would you still bake the cake?"

qa.q: What did Ines bake when a top mark went on the board?
qa.a: Honey cake.

qa.q: What was Olga worried about when she whispered to her pillow?
qa.a: That her mother's warmth, the cake and being called her little star, comes only with top marks, and that she would lose it for a low score.

qa.q: What could Ines change so that Olga stops hiding mistakes?
qa.a: Show warmth on ordinary evenings too and talk calmly about low marks, so love isn't tied to the fridge board.

qa.q: How might Ines feel if she found the spelling test in the bin?
qa.a: Ines would probably be hurt and alarmed, realising Olga was afraid enough to hide it, and might see that the board sent the wrong message.

grounding: A child whose mother celebrates only top marks hides a low score, fearing love depends on performance.

passage:
Monday: The history project on the Mughal gardens was due on Friday. Harsha wrote the heading five times on fresh chart paper; each time a letter leaned slightly. Her sister Gargi watched the pile of crumpled sheets grow. "It looks fine!" "It doesn't. It has to be perfect."
Wednesday: Harsha had one good page, then smudged a line and rubbed at it until the paper tore through. She sat on the floor holding the hole up to the light and didn't say anything for a long time.
Friday: The class handed in their projects. Harsha handed in nothing. "I'll bring it Monday, ma'am," she said. At home she told Gargi, "If it's not perfect, it's worse than not giving it." Gargi said, "But nothing gets zero."

qa.q: How many times did Harsha write the heading on Monday?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: Why does Harsha feel handing in nothing is better than an imperfect project?
qa.a: Her standard is so high that anything less than perfect feels like failing, so not submitting seems less painful than being judged.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Harsha on Wednesday?
qa.a: Patching the tear or starting the page again with a time limit, and handing in a finished "good enough" version rather than nothing.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the week?
qa.a: Gargi watches the crumpled sheets pile up and thinks the work already looked fine, and is puzzled that nothing is better than something.

grounding: A teenager rewrites a project page until the paper tears and hands in nothing because it is not perfect.

passage: Vijay, you've rewritten that essay four times. Let me tell you about your Nani at fifteen. A teacher once said, "Preeti, your handwriting is the best in the class," and after that every page had to be flawless. If one letter was wrong, I'd tear the whole page out and start again. For my final-year geography record, I redrew the first map eleven times. The eraser went through the paper, twice. The night before submission I had one perfect map and forty empty pages. I didn't submit it. I told the teacher I was ill. I thought a missing record was better than a messy one. It wasn't, beta. It cost me the marks, and nobody ever saw the map. Hand yours in. Messy is finished.

qa.q: How many times did young Preeti redraw the first map?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did young Preeti think a missing record was better than a messy one?
qa.a: After the teacher's praise, anything less than flawless felt like losing that identity, so not submitting seemed safer than showing imperfect work.

qa.q: What choice does Nani urge Vijay to make?
qa.a: To hand the essay in now, even messy, because finishing matters more than a perfect page nobody sees.

qa.q: What might Vijay feel hearing that Nani did the same thing?
qa.a: Vijay may feel understood and less ashamed of the rewriting, and more willing to stop, since Nani knows exactly where it leads.

grounding: A grandmother recalls redrawing a map until the paper tore at fifteen and handing in nothing.

passage: The drawing exam gave each Class 11 student one sheet of cartridge paper and two hours. Jomon began a still life of a jug and three onions. The jug's curve looked wrong. He erased it. Drew it again. Erased. By the end of the first hour the paper had gone grey and fuzzy where the jug should be. Avni, at the next easel, had finished her outline and started shading. Jomon pressed harder with the eraser, and the sheet ripped in a jagged line. There was no second sheet. He stared at the tear, then quietly put his pencils away. When the invigilator collected the papers, his was blank except for the torn grey patch. Outside, Avni asked what happened. "It wasn't good enough," he said. "Nothing would've been good enough."

qa.q: What was Jomon drawing?
qa.a: A still life of a jug and three onions.

qa.q: What does "Nothing would've been good enough" reveal about Jomon's mind?
qa.a: His standard was so high that no drawing could meet it, so stopping felt less painful than finishing something he'd judge a failure.

qa.q: What could Jomon try in the next timed exam?
qa.a: Allow the first outline to stand, move on to the onions and shading, and fix only at the end, so a whole drawing gets finished.

qa.q: How might Avni feel seeing Jomon's torn blank sheet?
qa.a: Avni may feel shocked and sad, having watched a capable classmate erase his way to nothing while she moved on to shading.

grounding: Under exam time pressure, a teenager erases a drawing until the paper tears and submits nothing.

passage:
"Ankita, it's two in the morning. Still on the lab report?"
"Just checking the formatting, Ma."
Jyoti sat on the bed. "You checked it at dinner too."
"There might be a mistake."
"And if there is?"
Ankita's hands stopped on the keyboard. "Then they'll see."
"See what?"
"That I'm normal. Everyone's always said I'm the one who never makes mistakes. Since school. You, Papa, my teachers."
Jyoti was quiet. "We said that because we were proud."
"I know. But now if I get one thing wrong, I'm just ordinary."
"Do you even like chemistry anymore?"
Ankita laughed shakily. "I don't know. I don't have time to think about liking it. I'm too busy not failing."
Jyoti closed the laptop gently. "Ordinary is allowed in this house."

qa.q: What was Ankita still checking at two in the morning?
qa.a: The formatting of the lab report.

qa.q: What is Ankita afraid a single mistake would show?
qa.a: That Ankita is ordinary; the family's pride in never making mistakes has become something to protect, so fear drives the checking more than love of chemistry.

qa.q: What choice by Jyoti helps, and why?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and saying ordinary is allowed, which separates Ankita's worth at home from flawless work.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel on hearing "too busy not failing"?
qa.a: Jyoti seems saddened to realise the family's proud praise became a weight, and wants to lift it.

grounding: A student praised for never making mistakes checks work obsessively, driven by fear of seeming ordinary.

passage: I've been the "perfect one" since Class 4, when my teacher held up my notebook as the model for the whole school. After that, every page, every test, every project had to be flawless. In college it got worse. I'd spend three nights on a two-page assignment, not because I loved the topic but because I was terrified of the one red mark that would prove I was just average. My friend Manoj once asked, "Dhruv, do you actually enjoy economics?" I didn't know how to answer. I think I used to. Somewhere the love got replaced by fear. Last month I handed in an essay with a typo on page one, by accident. Nothing happened. The professor gave it an A. I felt oddly empty, and oddly free.

qa.q: How long would Dhruv spend on a two-page assignment?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel empty and free after the typo essay got an A?
qa.a: The feared disaster didn't happen, which exposed how much of the effort was fear; that was unsettling and a relief at once.

qa.q: What choice could Dhruv make with the next assignment?
qa.a: Set a time limit and submit a solid version on purpose, to test again whether small flaws really prove anything.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Dhruv's hard work?
qa.a: Manoj seems to sense that Dhruv's striving comes from pressure rather than enjoyment, and the question suggests real concern.

grounding: A student praised since childhood for flawless work strives out of fear of being average rather than love of the subject.

passage:
Teacher's note, Hafsa, Kathak senior batch, 4 March
Noor has been with me since she was eight, and for years everyone, including me, praised her as "flawless". Today in rehearsal she missed one turn in the new piece, stopped dead and asked to leave. In the corridor she was shaking. She said, "If I make mistakes on stage, people will see I'm just average. That's all I have." I've noticed she hasn't smiled while dancing for months; she dances as if she's sitting an exam. I think our praise may have taught her that her worth lies in never slipping.
What I did: I asked her to dance the piece once for me with the goal of enjoying it, not getting it right, and told her plainly that I value her whether she slips or not. We'll try again on Thursday.

qa.q: What happened when Noor missed one turn in rehearsal?
qa.a: She stopped dead and asked to leave, and was shaking in the corridor.

qa.q: Why does one missed turn feel so dangerous to Noor?
qa.a: Years of being called flawless made perfection feel like her whole value, so a slip seems to prove she is only average.

qa.q: Which choice by Hafsa addresses the fear behind the perfectionism?
qa.a: Asking her to dance once for enjoyment and saying clearly that she is valued whether she slips or not.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see her own part in Noor's fear?
qa.a: Hafsa admits the years of "flawless" praise, including her own, may have taught Noor that her worth depends on never slipping.

grounding: A dance teacher notes that a student long praised as flawless now dances out of fear of seeming ordinary.
